identity.name: Yugoslav Partisans
native_names: Narodnooslobodilačka vojska i partizanski odredi Jugoslavije

land.text: the new Yugoslavia: 'By the end of the war, the Partisans had gained control of the entire country as well as Trieste and Carinthia' (page A)

successors.note: The Partisan-held land of 1944 (corrected keyframe) passed to the Yugoslavia of the coalition government formed in Belgrade on 8 March 1945; the rest of Cliopatria's 1945 shape was taken in the spring campaigns of 1945 (Sarajevo in early April, the rest of the NDH and Slovenia through mid-May, page A), after this dossier ends. Cliopatria shares Wikidata Q83286 between its Yugoslavia and Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia rows, so the successor dossier is yugoslavia.

capitals.name: Foča
capitals.note: Page B: after the Second Enemy Offensive (January to early February 1942) the Partisans 'established a new headquarters at Foča'. The infobox of page A gives the headquarters as 'Mobile, attached to the Main Operational Group'; before 1942 and between the dated seats there was no fixed capital.

capitals.name: Drvar (Supreme Headquarters, mobile)
capitals.note: Page A: in September 1943 Fitzroy Maclean 'was parachuted to Tito's headquarters near Drvar'. The page does not date the move to Drvar or the departure from it; 1944 is held as the last year of the western Bosnian seat, with Belgrade only from the March 1945 government.

capitals.name: Belgrade
capitals.note: Page B: 'On 8 March 1945, a coalition Yugoslav government was formed in Belgrade', with Tito as Premier. Belgrade was taken on 20 October 1944; the pages do not say when the headquarters moved there.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1944 Partisan shape plus the lands the page names for the onset of winter 1944: 'the entire eastern half of Yugoslavia - Serbia, Macedonia, Montenegro - as well as most of the Dalmatian coast' (page B; page A: 'Serbia, Vardar Macedonia and Montenegro, as well as the Dalmatian coast')

keyframe_review.note: Neither page gives a km2 figure for the Partisans (the infobox of page A has none). Cliopatria's 33,803 km2 (123 grid cells, 13% of its 250,300 km2 Yugoslavia of 1945) covers 42 of Montenegro's 50 cells, parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and the Zlatibor district of Serbia, and 62 of the 64 cells the NDH loses between its 1943 and 1944 shapes; it holds neither Belgrade nor Macedonia nor the Dalmatian ports. Page B says that by late 1944 the Partisans controlled the eastern half of Yugoslavia plus most of the Dalmatian coast, about 125,000 km2 on the 1945 total, so Cliopatria's shape is about 0.27 of the page's extent, beyond a factor of two: the shape is too small for the end of 1944. The correction adds Serbia, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Dalmatia (about 146,000 km2 by grid cells, 0.57 of the 1945 Yugoslavia). Caveats for the renderer: Syrmia was a German and NDH front until 1945 (ledger contest, page B); Kosovo and Vojvodina are not named by the pages; Dalmatia is taken whole where the page says 'most'. The correction is the end-of-1944 extent; the ledger dates the gains inside the year (Belgrade 20 October, the rest at the onset of winter).

region.text: the Brezovica woods between Sisak and Zagreb

ledger.note: 22 June 1941: the first Partisan uprising, in the Brezovica woods between Sisak and Zagreb. Page A: 'The first Partisan uprising occurred in Croatia on 22 June 1941'; 'The Communist Party of Yugoslavia formally decided to launch an armed uprising on 4 July'; 'On 27 July 1941, a Partisan-led uprising began in the area of Drvar and Bosansko Grahovo.' The infobox gives 'Dates active: 1941-1945'. The page names woods, not a boundary; the county is the gazetteer's nearest unit.

region.text: the liberated west of Serbia around Užice

ledger.note: 17 November 1941: the Main National Liberation Committee for Serbia is founded in Užice, seat of the short-lived republic of the liberated west. Page A: 'A short-lived republic was created in the liberated west, the first liberated territory in Europe'; the committee was 'founded in Užice on 17 November 1941'. The page does not date the republic's creation or give its extent; the Zlatibor district (which holds Užice) is the researcher's reading, and the date is the earliest the page gives for its government. [Reviewer eu-21-e: re-dated from November to 24 September 1941 on the Republic of Užice page, whose infobox gives 'Fall of Užice: 24 September 1941' and whose first sentence says the republic 'existed in the autumn of 1941'; the same page bounds it by 'the river Drina on the west, the river Zapadna Morava in the east' and gives 15,000 or 20,000 km2, so the Zlatibor district alone is too small.]

region.text: the liberated west of Serbia around Užice

ledger.note: By 29 November 1941: German forces suppress the uprising and the republic of Užice, the first liberated territory in Europe, falls. Page A: 'The uprising was suppressed by German forces by 29 November 1941.' Page B: 'Germany occupied Serbia outright.'

1942: after the Second Enemy Offensive (January to early February) the Partisan headquarters moves to Foča. Page B: the Partisans 'established a new headquarters at Foča'; the year follows from the offensive's dates, the page's sentence has no year of its own.

4 November 1942: the Partisans win at Bihać and found the so-called Bihać Republic in the heart of the NDH. Page B: the victory at Bihać on 4 November 1942 allowed them to 'establish the so-called Bihać Republic'; the first session of AVNOJ met at Bihać on 26-27 November 1942. The page gives no extent; the Una-Sana canton is the researcher's reading of the Bihać area, and the republic reached beyond it.

January to April 1943: the Fourth Enemy Offensive drives the Partisans out of western Bosnia and the Bihać Republic. Page B: the Fourth Enemy Offensive (Battle of the Neretva, Operation Weiss) pushed the Partisans from western Bosnia toward the Neretva, 'This took place from January to April, 1943'; page A (first read) places it 'against the Republic of Bihać'. Neither page says which towns fell or when, so the loss of the Una-Sana area is the researcher's bridge. [Reviewer eu-21-e: confidence raised to 2: page B dates the offensive 'from January to April, 1943' and says 'Axis forces pushed Partisan troops to retreat from western Bosnia to northern Herzegovina'; the year and the land are the page's, the Una-Sana unit is the researcher's reading.]

By September 1943: Tito's headquarters are near Drvar in western Bosnia. Page A: in September 1943 Fitzroy Maclean 'was parachuted to Tito's headquarters near Drvar'; the page does not say when the headquarters moved there.

October to December 1944: the Partisans, with British artillery, stem the Germans and liberate Risan and Podgorica, taking Montenegro. Page B: 'The Partisans with British artillery were able to stem the Germans and liberated Risan and Podgorica between October and December'; the sentence has no year of its own and the surrounding text places it in 1944. Page B: after Italy's capitulation the former Italian kingdom 'of Montenegro' was 'placed under German occupation'. Cliopatria draws no state on Montenegro in 1941-43.

region.text: the land the NDH holds in 1943 and no longer in 1944

ledger.note: 1944: the Partisan-held interior of the NDH, the land its 1944 shape no longer holds. Cliopatria shrinks the Independent State of Croatia from 96,150 km2 (1941-43) to 78,716 km2 (1944) just as the Partisan shape appears, and 62 of the 64 cells lost lie inside it; neither page opened dates an NDH loss in 1944. Page B puts the Partisans 'in the heart of the NDH' from November 1942 and page A in 'parts of Bosnia' in the middle of the war. A bridge from the Cliopatria shapes; a gap-filler should open the pages on the 1944 front in Bosnia and Lika.

20 October 1944: the Red Army and the Partisans liberate Belgrade in the Belgrade Offensive. Page A: 'On 20 October, the Red Army and the Partisans liberated Belgrade in a joint operation known as the Belgrade Offensive'; the same paragraph opens 'in the second half of 1944 the Partisans turned their attention to Serbia'.

Winter 1944: the Partisans control Serbia. Page A: 'At the onset of winter, the Partisans effectively controlled the entire eastern half of Yugoslavia', naming 'Serbia, Vardar Macedonia and Montenegro, as well as the Dalmatian coast'. Month 12 is the researcher's reading of 'onset of winter'; the pages give no dates for the towns of Serbia. Page B: 'Germany occupied Serbia outright'. Cliopatria's 1944 shapes give Serbia mostly to Nazi Germany (225 of 283 cells), with 27 cells in Bulgaria's and 14 in the NDH's. Syrmia stays a front (contest below).

Winter 1944: Vardar Macedonia, North Macedonia today, passes to the Partisans. Page A: the Partisans controlled 'Serbia, Vardar Macedonia and Montenegro' at the onset of winter 1944; page B: 'Bulgaria formally annexed these territories on 14 May 1941'. Neither page describes the transfer. Cliopatria's 1944 Bulgaria still holds 88 of North Macedonia's 93 cells, hence the counterpart.

Winter 1944: the Partisans hold most of the Dalmatian coast. Page B: 'By this time the Partisans effectively controlled the entire eastern half of Yugoslavia - Serbia, Macedonia, Montenegro - as well as most of the Dalmatian coast' (October to December 1944). Page B (first read): Italy's Dalmatian possessions were divided between Germany and the NDH, hence the counterpart; the page gives no town dates, and the whole region is taken where it says 'most'.

Winter 1944: the front in Syrmia freezes between the Partisans and the Wehrmacht and NDH forces. Page B: 'The Wehrmacht and the forces of the Ustaše-controlled Independent State of Croatia fortified a front in Syrmia that held through the winter of 1944-45.' The page does not date the front's creation; month 12 is read from 'held through the winter'. The NDH forces are named in the note because a counterpart is one string.

1945: the Syrmian Front ends. The page says only that the front 'held through the winter of 1944-45'; the date of the breakthrough is not on the pages opened, so the year is the researcher's bridge and the end falls under the successor Yugoslavia.
8 March 1945: the coalition government meets in Belgrade. Page B: 'On 8 March 1945, a coalition Yugoslav government was formed in Belgrade' with Tito as Premier.

region.text: the land held by the Partisans (the corrected 1944 keyframe), which passes to the new Yugoslavia

ledger.note: March 1945: the Partisans merge into the Yugoslav state: the National Liberation Army becomes the Yugoslav Army on 1 March and a coalition government forms in Belgrade on 8 March. Page B: 'On 8 March 1945, a coalition Yugoslav government was formed in Belgrade'; page A: 'on 1 March 1945, the National Liberation Army was transformed into the regular armed forces of Yugoslavia.' The Tito-Šubašić agreement between the Partisans and the government-in-exile of Peter II was signed on the island of Vis on 16 June 1944 (page B). Whether this is the end of a 'state' is the researcher's reading; the pages call the successor 'Democratic Federal Yugoslavia'.

wars.name: Partisan uprising of 1941 in western Serbia (Republic of Užice)

zones.text: the liberated west of Serbia, Užice

wars.outcome: German forces suppressed the uprising by 29 November 1941 and the short-lived republic of the liberated west fell.
wars.note: The article title of the war was not opened; the name is descriptive. Page A: 'The uprising was suppressed by German forces by 29 November 1941.'

wars.name: Fourth Enemy Offensive (Battle of the Neretva)
belligerents: Axis forces and the NDH (named only as 'the enemy' in the extracts read)
wars.outcome: The offensive pushed the Partisans from western Bosnia toward the Neretva; 'This took place from January to April, 1943.'
wars.note: The belligerents beyond the Partisans were not read from the page text; confirm on the war's own article.

wars.name: Seventh Enemy Offensive (Operation Rösselsprung)
wars.outcome: An unsuccessful attempt to eliminate Tito personally, in western Bosnia in the second quarter of 1944 (late May); no border moved.
wars.note: Page A: 'the final attack in western Bosnia in the second quarter of 1944'; page B: 'Operation Rösselsprung in late May 1944'. Drvar is not named for the raid on either page extract.

wars.name: Belgrade Offensive
wars.outcome: The Red Army and the Partisans liberated Belgrade on 20 October 1944 and the Partisans then controlled Serbia.
wars.note: Page B: 'The Red Army organised the Belgrade Offensive, and took the city on 20 October.'

wars.name: Syrmian Front
wars.outcome: The Wehrmacht and NDH forces fortified a front in Syrmia that held through the winter of 1944-45.
wars.note: The front's start and the breakthrough are not dated on the pages opened; the war is named for the page's 'front in Syrmia'.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line bounds the Partisans: liberated areas, guerrilla zones and fronts are approximate. The Tito-Šubašić agreement of 16 June 1944 (page B) fixed no frontier. The frontier of the corrected 1944 keyframe along Syrmia is a front line, softer still.

notes:
Page budget: two pages (Yugoslav Partisans; World War II in Yugoslavia), the budget for a 1-shape state; the extracts were taken by WebFetch, which answers from a summariser, so the quotes are the extract's rendering of the page. Not opened and needed by a gap-filler: 'Democratic Federal Yugoslavia' and 'Second session of AVNOJ' (the proclamation at Jajce on 29 November 1943 is not on either page extract; Jajce, Drvar raid and Vis as seats are 'page silent'), 'Republic of Užice', 'Bihać Republic', 'Operation Rösselsprung', 'Belgrade Offensive', 'Syrmian Front', and the pages on the Italian armistice of 8 September 1943 (page B only says two Italian divisions joined the Montenegrin Partisans, not that land passed to them).

Decisions. (1) Life 1941-1945: page A's infobox gives 'Dates active: 1941-1945'; Cliopatria maps only 1944. The only mapped keyframe is therefore 1944 (corrected, see keyframe_review). 1941-43 territory (Užice 1941, the Bihać Republic 1942-43) has ledger events but no keyframe, because the pages give no extent; the ledger regions there are the researcher's nearest administrative unit and the renderer should treat them as captions, not as outlines, until a gap-filler adds keyframes. The June 1942 sentence in page B ('By June the Partisans had lost practically all their free territory in eastern Bosnia, Montenegro and Herzegovina') is not mapped for the same reason. (2) 1945 belongs to the successor yugoslavia (Cliopatria's whole-country shape); draw this dossier through 1944 only, the end date March 1945 carries the dissolution caption. (3) type is rebel (resistance movement holding liberated land against the Axis and the NDH, drawn hatched until it wins); it also ran the Democratic Federal Yugoslavia of page A's infobox, so a reviewer may prefer state; the family balkans is the researcher's choice. (4) Predecessors are empty because the pages do not say whose land the first uprising took (the Sisak county of the founding event lay in the NDH, which is not on the pages). (5) Gains from nazi-germany in Montenegro and Serbia stand in for Axis occupation zones Cliopatria lacks (the scope of eu-21 names Serbia and Montenegro as occupations to be added by eu-21-x); when those dossiers exist the counterparts should be repointed. Cliopatria draws Montenegro 1941-43 as no state.

Not from the pages: the native names (Serbo-Croat forms, researcher's knowledge) and the capitals' coordinates. Places absent from the gazetteer and not needed as region specs: Drvar, Bihać, Užice, Risan, Vis, Jajce (the admin-1 units Una-Sana, Zlatiborski, Grad Beograd, Sisacko-Moslavacka stand in). Kosovo and Vojvodina are not named by the pages for 1944; Cliopatria's Albania shape is the counterpart candidate for Kosovo and was not checked.

Cliopatria row check: one row, one shape (1944, 33,803 km2); no row to split or merge. Its neighbours list (albania, independent-state-of-croatia, nazi-germany, principality-of-bulgaria) is covered by counterparts in the ledger except albania, which the pages opened do not mention in a territorial event.
